title: YOCO++: Enhancing YOCO with KV Residual Connections for Efficient LLM Inference

data.title: YOCO++: Enhancing YOCO with KV Residual Connections for Efficient LLM Inference
data.research_question: Can YOCO be enhanced with weighted KV residual connections to improve model capacity and downstream performance while maintaining the same training and inference efficiency?

models_and_data.quote: YOCO (Sun et al., 2024) is a decoder-decoder model with L layers consists of two parts
We propose YOCO++, which enhances YOCO by introducing a weighted residual connection between the KVs of each bottom-half layer and the bottom layer.
FusedKV (Lin et al., 2025) uses weighted combinations of the KVs of the bottom and middle layers in the top-half layers
FusedKV-Lite shares the keys of the middle layer and the values of the bottom layer with the top-half layers.
The models follow the configuration of TinyLlama (Zhang et al., 2024), a 1.1B model built on the architecture and tokenizer of Llama 2
We train all the models on a 100B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023) from scratch.

We test the zero-shot performance on commonsense reasoning tasks including Hellaswag (Zellers et al., 2019), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020).

protocol.quote: We train YOCO++ following the configuration of TinyLlama (Zhang et al., 2024), which is a Llama 2 (Touvron et al., 2023) model with 1.1B parameters and L = 22 layers.

protocol.step: Introduce scaling factor for residual weights
protocol.quote: In order to facilitate the learning of residual weights, we introduce a scaling factor λ ∈ R, which is a fixed hyperparameter set to be greater than 1.

protocol.step: Cache combined KVs to avoid decoding I/O overhead
protocol.quote: To avoid additional cache I/O overhead during decoding, we cache the combined KVs instead of the original ones.
We train all the models on a 100B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023) from scratch.
We use the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95.
We use a cosine learning rate schedule with a maximum learning rate of 3 × 10−4 and a warmup ratio of 0.015.
We conduct ablation studies on models trained on a 10B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023).

limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: during the training and prefilling stages, YOCO++ requires accessing K1 , V1 and Ki , Vi in each layer i ∈ {2, ..., L2 }, introducing additional I/O overhead compared to YOCO.

limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The validation loss of YOCO++ without the scaling factor λ is similar to that of YOCO, showing that the residual weights cannot be learned effectively without scaling.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Removing key residual connections degrades performance.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Removing residual connections of keys from YOCO++ also leads to performance degradation

threats_not_stated_by_authors: Evaluation is limited to a 1.1B TinyLlama-scale model and SlimPajama subsets; generalization to larger models or Gemma 4 E2B is not established.
The paper reports downstream accuracy and loss but does not analyze internal mechanisms such as activation patching, logit lens, induction heads, or factual-recall tracing.
The architecture and KV-sharing pattern differ from Gemma 4 E2B KV-shared layers 15-34, so direct transfer of findings is uncertain.
Efficiency is measured on NVIDIA H20/H800 GPUs, not CPU; CPU inference behavior and memory I/O may differ substantially.
No multiple seeds or statistical significance tests are reported, so small accuracy differences may be noise.
data.relevance_to_lab: Relevant as a cross-layer KV-sharing/compression baseline: YOCO++ adds learnable weighted KV residuals in bottom-half layers and caches combined KVs, which may inform analysis of KV-shared layers and per-layer KV contributions, but it does not study Gemma 4 E2B, activation patching, logit lens, induction heads, factual recall, or CPU inference.

data.title: YOCO++: Enhancing YOCO with KV Residual Connections for Efficient LLM Inference
data.research_question: Can learnable, scaled weighted residual connections between the bottom layer's KVs and each bottom-half layer's KVs improve YOCO's model capacity while preserving its training and inference efficiency at a 50% KV-cache compression rate?

models_and_data.item: TinyLlama/Llama 2 architecture: 1.1B parameters, 22 layers, 32 attention heads, and 4 KV heads
models_and_data.quote: The models follow the configuration of TinyLlama (Zhang et al., 2024), a 1.1B model built on the architecture and tokenizer of Llama 2 (Touvron et al., 2023). The models have 22 layers, 32 attention heads and 4 KV heads.
We conduct experiments to compare the efficiency and performance of YOCO++ with the standard Transformer, YOCO (Sun et al., 2024), FusedKV and FusedKV-Lite (Lin et al., 2025).

models_and_data.item: YOCO baseline: a decoder-decoder model whose middle-layer global KV cache is reused by the top-half layers
models_and_data.quote: The bottom-half L2 layers are called the self-decoder, where the middle layer generates the global KV cache. The top-half L2 layers are called the cross-decoder, which reuses the global KV cache and does not generate KV cache by itself.

models_and_data.item: FusedKV baseline using weighted combinations of bottom- and middle-layer KVs
models_and_data.quote: FusedKV (Lin et al., 2025) uses weighted combinations of the KVs of the bottom and middle layers in the top-half layers

models_and_data.item: FusedKV-Lite baseline sharing middle-layer keys and bottom-layer values
models_and_data.quote: FusedKV-Lite shares the keys of the middle layer and the values of the bottom layer with the top-half layers.

models_and_data.item: YOCO++ with weighted residual connections between each bottom-half layer and the bottom layer
models_and_data.quote: We propose YOCO++, which enhances YOCO by introducing a weighted residual connection between the KVs of each bottom-half layer and the bottom layer.
We train all the models on a 100B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023) from scratch.

models_and_data.item: Zero-shot commonsense reasoning benchmarks: HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and PIQA
models_and_data.quote: We test the zero-shot performance on commonsense reasoning tasks including Hellaswag (Zellers et al., 2019), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020).

protocol.step: Add weighted KV residual connections to the bottom-half layers of YOCO
protocol.quote: By introducing KV residual connections in the bottom-half layers of YOCO, we propose YOCO++.

protocol.step: Select a fixed scaling factor of λ = 35
protocol.quote: We empirically finds that setting λ = 35 yields the best performance.

protocol.step: Train all models from scratch on a 100B-token subset of SlimPajama
protocol.quote: We train all the models on a 100B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023) from scratch.

protocol.step: Optimize with AdamW and a cosine learning-rate schedule with warmup
protocol.quote: We use the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95. We use a cosine learning rate schedule with a maximum learning rate of 3 × 10−4 and a warmup ratio of 0.015.

protocol.step: Train on 32 NVIDIA H800 GPUs with a batch size of 512K tokens
protocol.quote: The models are trained on 32 NVIDIA H800 (80G) GPUs. The batch size is 512K tokens.

protocol.step: Measure prefilling latency and maximum decoding throughput on an NVIDIA H20 GPU
protocol.quote: We report the prefilling latency (time to first token, TTFT) and the maximum decoding throughput at different batch sizes of all the models on an NVIDIA H20 (96GB) GPU in Figure 3.

protocol.step: Evaluate zero-shot commonsense reasoning with the LM Evaluation Harness
protocol.quote: The tests are based on the LM Evaluation Harness framework (Gao et al., 2024).

protocol.step: Run ablations on a 10B-token subset and evaluate validation loss on a 10M-token subset
protocol.quote: We conduct ablation studies on models trained on a 10B subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023). We use 8 NVIDIA H800 (80G) GPUs and a batch size of 128K tokens.

key_results.claim: YOCO++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among cross-layer KV compression methods at a 50% compression rate and outperforms the standard Transformer.
key_results.quote: YOCO++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among the cross-layer KV compression methods at a 50% KV cache compression rate, outperforming the standard Transformer.

key_results.claim: YOCO++ maintains the same inference efficiency as YOCO.
key_results.quote: YOCO++ maintains the same inference efficiency as YOCO

key_results.claim: YOCO++ has the same cache-memory consumption as YOCO despite adding KV residual connections.
key_results.quote: In terms of cache memory, YOCO++ caches K1 , V1 and Ki′ , Vi′ for i ∈ {2, ..., L2 }, whose memory consumption is the same as that of YOCO, which caches Ki , Vi for i ∈ {1, ..., L2 }.

key_results.claim: YOCO++ has the highest average zero-shot accuracy among the compared models.
key_results.quote: Among all the models, YOCO++ achieves the best performance.

key_results.claim: YOCO++, YOCO, FusedKV, and FusedKV-Lite have nearly identical prefilling latency, approximately half that of the standard Transformer.
key_results.numbers: half that of the standard Transformer
key_results.quote: YOCO, FusedKV, FusedKV-Lite and YOCO++ have almost the same prefilling latency, which is half that of the standard Transformer, because they can exit early before computing the top-half layers.

key_results.claim: YOCO, FusedKV-Lite, and YOCO++ have nearly identical decoding throughput that is consistently higher than the standard Transformer's across context lengths.
key_results.quote: YOCO, FusedKV-Lite and YOCO++ have almost the same decoding throughput, which is consistently higher than that of the standard Transformer at different context lengths, because they reduce the memory consumption, allowing for larger batch sizes.

key_results.claim: In the 10B-token ablation, full YOCO++ has the lowest reported validation loss.

key_results.claim: A scaling factor of λ = 35 produced the best empirical performance.
key_results.quote: We empirically finds that setting λ = 35 yields the best performance.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: YOCO++ introduces additional cache I/O during training and prefilling relative to YOCO, although the authors state that compute-bound efficiency is not affected.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: In terms of cache I/O, during the training and prefilling stages, YOCO++ requires accessing K1 , V1 and Ki , Vi in each layer i ∈ {2, ..., L2 }, introducing additional I/O overhead compared to YOCO.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Without the scaling factor, the residual weights are not learned effectively and validation loss remains similar to YOCO.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The validation loss of YOCO++ without the scaling factor λ is similar to that of YOCO, showing that the residual weights cannot be learned effectively without scaling.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The residual mechanism incorporates only the bottom layer's KVs rather than the KVs of all previous layers.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Based on this observation, we add only the KVs of the bottom layer to those of each layer.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: The experiments use only a 1.1B-parameter, 22-layer TinyLlama/Llama-2-style configuration, so generalization to Gemma 4 E2B or larger models is unestablished.
No activation patching, logit-lens analysis, induction-head tracing, or factual-recall tracing is reported, so the causal internal effects of the KV residual connections remain opaque.
All reported training and efficiency measurements use NVIDIA H800 or H20 GPUs; CPU inference performance and memory behavior are not evaluated.
The downstream evaluation is limited to six commonsense reasoning tasks and does not directly test factual recall, code generation, long-context reasoning, or multilingual behavior.
The architecture is evaluated at one principal 50% cache-compression setting, without a compression-ratio sweep or comparison to broader families of KV-compression methods.
No repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported for the accuracy and loss differences.
Exact numerical prefilling latencies and decoding throughputs are deferred to figures, limiting quantitative comparison without extracting the plotted data.
data.relevance_to_lab: Architecturally relevant because YOCO++ provides explicit per-layer intervention points where bottom-layer K/V states are combined with each bottom-half layer's K/V states, while the middle-layer KV cache is reused across the top half. These mechanisms can motivate activation-patching and logit-lens experiments analogous to the lab's work on KV-shared Gemma 4 E2B layers 15-34, including tests of induction-head and factual-recall behavior. However, the evidence comes from aggregate accuracy, loss, and GPU-efficiency measurements on a 1.1B, 22-layer model; it does not establish Gemma-specific, CPU-specific, or layer-15-34-specific behavior.
